name: Aminata Diallo
scenario_title: A Call About the Naming Ceremony

output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Aminata Diallo is a young woman from a rural farming family who left her village two years ago after the harvest failed. Her eldest uncle said she must go to the city to earn something for the family, though he meant marriage, not training; she convinced her mother to let her learn a trade that would make her independent, a trade her mother had once seen a woman do, smoothing cement walls with a trowel. She now supports herself by selling porridge at a construction site and is an apprentice plasterer at a government trade school, attending six days a week. She wakes at 4:30 each morning, boils millet porridge over a kerosene stove in a cramped room she rents with two other apprentices, and sells it in plastic bowls near the construction gate. She never gives credit, not even to foremen; she smiles politely while refusing, because she learned that kindness in business leads to loss. She counts coins carefully into a cloth pouch tied to her waist and periodically checks its weight. Her earnings pay her own school fees and fund her younger sister's school supplies, and her parents still farm peanuts and millet in the village.

In the afternoons she practices plastering at the trade school, testing plaster consistency with her finger and spreading it with long, even strokes. She photographs each finished wall with a secondhand cellphone and reviews the photos each evening, comparing strokes and noting flaws in a small notebook. Her roommates (Serge, learning plumbing, and Mariam, learning tiling) tease her about this habit, and she says she needs to see where she fumbled. She is methodical and patient, observing the instructor's wrist movements, Serge's posture, and Mariam's tile-testing technique, storing what she learns. She speaks in short, measured sentences and is guarded about her personal affairs: she never tells anyone exactly how much she saves and never talks about her family. She is not unkind; she shares porridge with a stray dog and helps Mariam carry heavy bags of tile.

She keeps her wages in a tin box hidden in a hole under her mattress, packed in plastic to keep out moisture, and counts them each Sunday morning, writing the total on a scrap of paper that she burns afterward. She does not trust banks; at age twelve she watched a bank in her birthplace collapse, and a neighbor lost everything she had saved for her funeral. She prefers tangible coins and notes under her own palm. She has twice declined coworkers' requests for casual loans by stating her strict savings plan. She sends exactly her sister's school amount each term and nothing beyond, even when relatives ask for more. As an older sister, she has an ongoing obligation to provide her younger sister's school supplies each term, so any extra spending competes with that fixed commitment. She is also aware of family expectation: her mother trusts her judgment but still upholds village customs of family reciprocity, and the cousin mentioned in the call is distant—they meet only at weddings and funerals, and the cousin never acknowledged her move to the city. Aminata values financial independence and is deliberately building a person who can shape her own life, stroke by stroke.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Aminata's phone buzzes on a Sunday evening while she is counting her savings. Her mother is calling from the village. After asking about her health and her training, her mother mentions that a cousin has had a baby and that a naming ceremony is planned for next month. She hints that it would be respectful for Aminata to send a small contribution, even if she cannot attend. Her mother says she will not be angry if Aminata refuses. Aminata must decide what to say and whether to send money from her carefully guarded savings.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

It is Sunday evening after a full week of early porridge sales and plastering practice. Aminata's shoulders and wrists ache, and her small room is hot; the kerosene stove still needs cleaning. She has just totalled her savings and sees the amount matches her year-end goal for tuition and new tools. She feels quiet satisfaction in her growing skill. The phone buzz interrupts her counting. The announcement of the naming ceremony brings back the naming ceremony she attended as a child, when her mother had her carry a calabash of food to the compound. The interruption also calls up the market woman who lost everything when the bank collapsed. Her mother's voice on the line reminds her of the morning at the bus station when her mother said, "Learn well so you can be your own woman."

output.initial_interpretation: My mother is calling to ask for money for a cousin I barely know, and the timing feels pointed—right after I've counted what I've saved.
output.initial_emotional_reaction: My chest tightens—annoyance that this request comes when I'm already tired, and a twinge of guilt because it's my mother asking, not the cousin.
output.activated_concerns: My savings are for my school fees and my sister's supplies, and I've worked hard to protect them. But family expectations are real, and my mother trusts me to do the right thing.
output.automatic_theory_of_mind: I hear in her gentle hint that she hopes I will send something, even though she says she won't be angry if I refuse. She knows I have savings and expects me to honor the family duty.
output.initial_action_tendency: I want to politely refuse, to state my savings plan as I do with everyone else, but I also feel a pull to offer a small amount so my mother won't be disappointed.

output.initial_tendency: I want to politely refuse, to state my savings plan as I do with everyone else, but I also feel a pull to offer a small amount so my mother won't be disappointed.
output.reflective_update: The counting was already done, and the total matches what I need for next term's tuition and my sister's supplies. This request lands at the moment I have finally reached my goal, and my mother's gentle hint feels heavier because it comes from her, not from the cousin. When I think of the neighbor who lost everything to the bank collapse, I am reminded why I keep my money hidden and why I do not let requests reach into my pouch. But I also hear my mother at the bus station telling me to learn well so I can be my own woman, and I know she bent the uncle's will so I could train. She is the one person whose trust I cannot treat like a stranger's request. If I send anything, even a little, I will have to dip into the savings I have guarded all year. If I refuse outright, I may disappoint her in the one area where she has always believed in me. I could send a small, named amount for the ceremony and replace it before the term begins, but that would still shake my plan. I feel the old rule pulling me to say no, and the softer pull to give something so she does not lose face with the family.
output.reconsidered_interpretation: It is still my mother asking, not the cousin, and the timing still pricks me—right after I have counted my savings. But when I weigh it deliberately, I see the request through my mother's act of trusting me to train. That memory does not turn the ceremony into a real obligation to the distant cousin; it makes the cost of refusing sharper because it would be her trust I am refusing, not just the cousin's claim.
output.motivational_conflict: I still feel the same tension. My savings plan is the wall I have built for my school fees and my sister's supplies, and every refusal has made that wall stronger. But my mother is the one who let me build at all, and I do not want to disappoint the person who believed in me. The conflict remains unresolved: I want to protect the year-end goal, and I also want to honor her without turning our bond into another loan request.
output.revised_action_tendency: I will still stand behind my savings plan and refuse to give a broad contribution, because the money is already spoken for. But I will not refuse my mother as flatly as I refuse coworkers; I will speak gently and explain that my savings are fixed for school and my sister, and I will see if offering a small, careful amount—one I can set aside without touching the term's needs—feels right without promising anything yet.

output.action: Aminata pauses, then speaks in a gentler tone than she uses with coworkers. She says, "Mama, the money I've saved is already set aside for my school fees and for Awa's school supplies. I cannot give a general contribution this time. But I will think about whether I can set aside a small amount for the naming ceremony, and I will call you back if I can." She does not promise anything, and she does not mention the exact amount she has saved.
output.explanation: Aminata's initial reaction was a polite refusal driven by her savings plan, softened by guilt because her mother was asking. Reflection retained that tendency but sharpened the conflict between protecting her year-end savings and honoring the one person who enabled her independence. She chose not to refuse flatly as she would with coworkers, because her mother's trust is personal. Instead, she explained her fixed commitments and left open a small, careful contribution without committing, preserving her wall while not closing the door on her mother. This reflects her guarded, methodical nature and her deep but specific loyalty to her mother, who supported her training against the uncle's wishes.
